pages.text:
1. A Cousin Is Coming
2. Everything Is Different
3. The Camera Never Stops
4. A Small Disaster
5. Learning to Listen
6. The Best Kind of Day
7. Two Homes, One Family

The Visitor from Abroad is an original Tafiya Estate story. It shows two cousins from very different homes learning that curiosity works best when we put the camera down and truly join in. It celebrates family across distance, and the quiet lesson that every place, once you stop to look, has its own kind of wonder.

Chidera had never met her cousin Zainab, who had lived her whole life in London. Now Zainab and her mum were coming to spend the long holiday on the estate. For weeks the two girls had only waved at each other through video calls, the screen freezing at the funniest moments. At last the real day arrived, and Chidera could hardly sit still.

image.note: Chidera at a kitchen table, leaning close to a propped tablet showing a smiling girl's frozen video-call face mid-wave; Chidera bouncing with excitement; modern kitchen

pages.text: A car pulled up to the gate, and out climbed a girl with a neat suitcase and a phone already raised to film everything. "You must be Chidera," said Zainab, a little shy. "It's so hot here." Chidera laughed and hugged her. "You'll get used to it," she said. "Come on, I'll show you everything." And so the holiday began.

image.note: Zainab stepping out of a car at the estate gate, small suitcase in one hand, phone raised in the other; Chidera rushing to hug her; Remigius smiling from the gate

pages.text: To Zainab, everything on the estate was new and strange. She marvelled at the bright weaver birds nesting in the tall trees, and jumped when a gecko darted up the wall. She had never tasted a mango straight from the branch, its juice running warm down her wrist. "We only get these in shops," she said, amazed. Chidera just grinned.

image.note: Two girls under a mango tree in bright sun; Zainab holding a fresh mango, juice on her wrist, wide-eyed; a gecko on the wall behind; weaver-bird nests in the branches

pages.text: But some things puzzled Zainab. When the power cut out one afternoon, she gasped, but Chidera only fetched a lamp and carried on as if nothing had happened. When neighbours dropped by unannounced, Zainab whispered, "Did you know they were coming?" Chidera shook her head, smiling. "That's just how it is here," she said. "Everyone's family."

image.note: Dim room during a power cut, a small lamp glowing; Chidera calm and unbothered fetching it; Zainab startled; a neighbour and child appearing warmly at the open doorway

pages.text: Zainab filmed everything for her friends back home. The food, the birds, the market, the goats by the road. She held her phone up at meals and in the garden and even while Chidera was talking. Slowly, Chidera's smile began to fade. She had wanted a cousin to play with, not a camera pointed at her all day long.

image.note: Zainab holding her phone up to film a colourful market stall; Chidera beside her looking a little left out, arms folded; busy modern market behind them

pages.text: "You never just look," Chidera said at last, more sharply than she meant to. "You only film." Zainab's face went still. "I only wanted to show my friends," she said quietly, and slipped the phone into her pocket. An awkward silence sat between the cousins. Both girls felt they had somehow got it wrong, and neither knew how to make it right.

image.note: Two girls on a step, turned slightly away from each other; Zainab tucking her phone into her pocket, eyes down; Chidera looking regretful; a small uncomfortable gap between them

pages.text: The next morning, wanting to make peace, Zainab offered to help make lunch. But she had never cooked on a gas ring before, and she turned it up far too high. The oil in the pot hissed and spat and a black cloud of smoke went up. Chidera dashed in, switched off the gas, and threw open the window, coughing and laughing at once.

image.note: Kitchen with a smoking pot on a gas ring, thin black smoke rising; Zainab stepping back alarmed; Chidera lunging to switch off the gas and reaching for the window; comic panic, no flames

pages.text: When the smoke cleared, the two girls looked at the ruined, blackened lunch and burst out laughing until their sides ached. "In London I only ever use the microwave," Zainab admitted, wiping her eyes. "Then I'll teach you," said Chidera warmly. "And you can teach me about London." Just like that, the wall between them came tumbling down.

image.note: Two girls doubled over laughing beside a blackened pot; window open, smoke thinning; genuine warmth and relief between them

pages.text: That afternoon, Zainab put her phone away for good and truly joined in. She learned to pound and stir, getting flour on her nose. Chidera showed her how to call the weaver birds and where the sweetest mangoes hung. In return, Zainab taught Chidera London slang and the rules of a strange playground game, and both girls laughed at how odd the other's world could seem.

image.note: Two girls cooking together at a counter, flour on Zainab's nose, both laughing; the phone set aside, face-down and forgotten on the table; happy, easy

pages.text: "I was filming so much," Zainab said thoughtfully, "that I almost missed being here." Chidera nodded. "And I nearly forgot how strange all this must feel to you," she said. From then on they did everything together, two cousins from two far apart homes, discovering they were not so different after all.

image.note: The cousins sitting close on a veranda at golden hour, sharing a plate of mango slices, talking easily; the phone nowhere in sight; warm evening light

pages.text: For the estate's community day, the cousins cooked together as a team. Zainab brought a London pudding her mum had taught her, and Chidera made zobo, deep red and sweet. Side by side their two dishes sat on the long table, and neighbours tried both, nodding and reaching back for more. Nobody could say which they liked best.

image.note: A long community-day table; Zainab setting down a pudding beside Chidera's jug of deep-red zobo; smiling neighbours sampling both dishes; festive estate gathering

pages.text: When someone asked Zainab to say a few words, she did not reach for her phone. She simply stood and said, "Thank you for making me feel at home." The whole gathering clapped. Chidera squeezed her cousin's hand, prouder than she could say. It had turned out to be the very best kind of day.

image.note: Zainab standing to speak at the gathering, empty-handed and glowing; Chidera beside her squeezing her hand; a warm crowd clapping

pages.text: On the last morning, the girls swapped gifts. Zainab gave Chidera a red London bus, small enough to fit in a pocket. Chidera gave Zainab a carved wooden bird, like the weavers they had watched all summer. "Come and visit me next time," said Zainab. "I want to show you everything." Chidera grinned. "Now you sound like me," she said.

image.note: Close on the two gifts changing hands at the gate: a tiny red London bus and a carved wooden bird; both girls beaming; the waiting car behind

pages.text: The car pulled away, and Zainab waved from the window until the gate was out of sight. Chidera waved back, a little sad, but mostly glad. Two homes, one family, half a world apart and yet somehow side by side. She could not wait for the video call that night, freezing screen and all.

image.note: Chidera waving at the departing car from the gate, one hand up; the car window down with Zainab waving back; warm, bittersweet parting; Remigius by the gate
